Unit 1 — Introduction to Operations Research

1.1 Origin and growth of OR
Operations Research began in Britain during World War II, when military leaders needed to allocate scarce resources (radar,
aircraft, convoys) to many operations in the most effective way. Teams of scientists from engineering, mathematics, statistics,
economics and psychology studied search operations and flight patterns. After the war the same approach moved into industry
and business.

 Year Milestone

 1948 OR Club formed in England (later the OR Society of the U.K.)

 1950 OR Society of America formed; OR became an academic subject in the 1950s

 1953 OR unit set up at the Indian Statistical Institute, Calcutta

 1957 OR Society of India; Prof. Mahalanobis used OR for the Second Five Year Plan. International Federation of OR Societies formed



1.2 Definition and meaning

 Operations Research is the use of the scientific method, by an interdisciplinary team, to give managers a quantitative basis
 for decisions about man-machine-money systems, so that limited resources are used in the best possible way.


 ORSA: concerned with deciding how best to design and operate man-machine systems, usually needing allocation of scarce
 resources.
 Miller and Starr: OR is applied decision theory using scientific, mathematical and logical means.

 Daellenbach and George: a collection of mathematical techniques used with a systems approach to solve practical decision
 problems.
 Taha: a scientific approach by an interdisciplinary team to find the best use of limited resources.

 Thierauf and Klekamp: a planned approach by an interdisciplinary team to represent complex relationships as mathematical
 models for quantitative analysis.

Key terms: Operations are the activities of an organization; Research is observation and testing by the scientific method; a Model
is an abstract representation of reality; the Optimal solution maximizes or minimizes a measure of merit over all feasible
solutions; a Team brings varied skills to the problem.


1.3 Significant features of OR
 1. Decision-making tool: supplies a quantitative basis for choosing among alternatives.
 2. Scientific approach: observation, hypothesis, experiment, verification.

 3. Interdisciplinary team approach: no single discipline can handle every aspect of a large problem.
 4. Systems approach: the whole organization is studied, not one department, so sub-optimization is avoided.

 5. Use of digital computers: needed for the large calculations.

 6. Objective: finds the optimum, i.e. best possible, solution for the stated measure of effectiveness.

1.4 Concept of optimizing performance measure
Every OR model has a performance (effectiveness) measure such as profit, cost, time, distance or waiting time. Optimizing means
choosing the values of the controllable (decision) variables that maximize a measure like profit, or minimize a measure like cost,

subject to the constraints on resources. A simple model is E = f(Xc, Xuc) where E is effectiveness, Xc are controllable and

Xuc uncontrollable variables, with extra equations for constraints. The best value of E over all feasible choices is the optimal
solution.


1.5 Models in OR
A model is a theoretical approximation of a real problem. Its aim is to analyse the behaviour of the system so that performance
can be improved. Variables are controllable (decision) or uncontrollable (environment); a model also has result variables.

Operations Research - Theory Notes Page 5 of 31

5. Validate (test) the solution 6. Implement the solution 7. Modify the model 8. Establish control


 1. Problem formulation: study the physical system, state the objective, find constraints, controllable and uncontrollable
 variables, alternative actions and the measure of effectiveness.

 2. Model construction: express the measure of effectiveness and the constraints as functions of the variables, e.g. E = f(Xi,
 Yj).

 3. Input data: collect accurate data from reports, records and interviews. Quality of output depends on quality of data.

 4. Solution of the model: find the values of decision variables that optimize the objective by analytical, numerical or
 simulation methods. Sensitivity analysis is used if data are unstable.

 5. Validation: check that the model predicts the behaviour of the real system and includes all relevant objectives,
 constraints and variables.

 6. Implementation: convert the solution into workable instructions with management participation. If it is not
 implemented, the research is incomplete.

 7. Modification: revise the model if validation fails, adding omitted or correcting wrong constraints.

 8. Control: feedback on deviating variables so the solution stays valid under changing conditions.

 Why model formulation is crucial: every later phase depends on it. A wrong objective or a missing constraint gives a neat
 but useless answer however accurate the solver. It fixes what data are needed, which technique applies, and what the
 solution means. Mistakes found late are costly to correct, so most OR effort goes here.



1.9 Applications and limitations of OR
Applications: defence operations, industry and business (production, inventory, marketing, finance), government planning,
agriculture, hospitals, research and development, transport and logistics.

Limitations: models are only approximations of reality; good data are costly or unavailable; quantifying human or intangible
factors is difficult; cost of the OR study can exceed the benefit for small problems; managers may resist the results.

Unit 2 — Linear Programming Problem

2.1 Linear programming: meaning and formulation

 Linear Programming (LP) is a technique for optimizing (maximizing or minimizing) a linear objective function of decision
 variables subject to linear equality or inequality constraints and non-negativity restrictions.


Components: decision variables; objective function; constraints; non-negativity restrictions.

Steps of formulation: (1) identify the decision variables; (2) write the objective function in terms of them; (3) write each resource,
demand or requirement restriction as a linear constraint; (4) add non-negativity conditions.

Industrial examples: product mix (max profit with limited machine hours and material), blending (min cost meeting nutrient or
quality specifications), diet problem, production scheduling, cutting stock, portfolio selection.

General form: Max (or Min) Z = c1x1 + ... + cnxn subject to ai1x1 + ... + ainxn (≤, =, ≥) bi, xj ≥ 0.

Matrix form: Max Z = c x subject to A x (≤, =, ≥) b, x ≥ 0, where c is the 1×n cost vector, A the m×n coefficient matrix, b the m×1
requirement vector and x the n×1 decision vector.

Standard form: all constraints are equations with non-negative right-hand sides, all variables non-negative. A ≤ constraint gets a
slack variable, a ≥ constraint gets a surplus variable (subtracted). An unrestricted variable is replaced by the difference of two non-
negative variables. A minimization problem can be converted: Min Z = −Max(−Z).


2.2 Implicit assumptions of LP

 Assumption Meaning

 Proportionality (linearity) Contribution of a variable to the objective and constraints is directly proportional to its value

 Additivity Total effect is the sum of individual effects; no interaction between variables

 Divisibility Variables can take fractional values

 Certainty (deterministic) All coefficients cj, aij, bi are known constants

 Non-negativity Decision variables cannot be negative

 Finiteness A finite number of variables and constraints and a finite set of alternatives



2.3 Geometry of LP: hyperplane, convex set, extreme points, BFS
 Hyperplane: the set {x : a1x1 + ... + anxn = b}. It is a line in 2 dimensions and a plane in 3. It splits space into two half-spaces,
 and each ≤ or ≥ constraint is a half-space.
 Convex set: a set in which the line segment joining any two points of the set lies wholly in the set, i.e. x = λx1 + (1−λ)x2, 0 ≤ λ ≤
 1, is in the set. Intersection of convex sets is convex, so the feasible region of an LP is convex.

 Convex polyhedron: intersection of a finite number of half-spaces; a bounded one is a polytope.

 Extreme point (vertex): a point of a convex set that cannot be written as a convex combination of two other distinct points of
 the set. In the graph it is a corner point.



Operations Research - Theory Notes Page 7 of 31

Basic solution: for m equations in n unknowns (n > m), set n−m variables (non-basic) to zero and solve for the remaining m
 (basic). A basic feasible solution (BFS) is a basic solution with all variables ≥ 0. It is degenerate if a basic variable equals zero.
 There are at most nCm basic solutions.


 Fundamental theorems: (i) The feasible region of an LP is a convex set. (ii) If an optimal solution exists, it occurs at an
 extreme point. (iii) Every BFS corresponds to an extreme point and vice versa. Hence the simplex method only needs to
 search the extreme points, moving from one adjacent BFS to a better one.



2.4 Graphical method and its special cases
Steps: (1) treat each constraint as an equation and plot the line; (2) shade the side satisfying the inequality; (3) mark the common
(feasible) region; (4) find corner points; (5) evaluate Z at each corner, or draw the iso-profit/iso-cost line and slide it; (6) pick the
best corner. It works directly for two variables only.

 Special case How it appears

 Multiple (alternate) Objective line parallel to a binding constraint; every point on that edge is optimal
 optima

 Unbounded solution Feasible region is open in the direction of improvement, so Z can grow without limit. Signals a missing
 constraint in the model

 Infeasibility No point satisfies all constraints; feasible region is empty

 Redundant constraint Lies outside or along the feasible region and does not change it

 Degeneracy More than two constraint lines meet at a corner point



 Can a three-variable LPP (Max Z = 2x1 + 3x2 + 4x3, two ≤ constraints) be solved by the graphical method?
 10 marks (partly numerical) Re-exam Feb 2025

 MODEL ANSWER

 Not directly. The graphical method needs a plane with one axis per variable, so it handles only two decision variables. Three
 variables need a 3-D feasible region, which cannot be drawn and read reliably, and four or more cannot be drawn at all.

 Alternatives: (a) use the simplex method, which works for any number of variables; (b) convert to the dual. The number of
 dual variables equals the number of primal constraints. Here there are two constraints, so the dual has two variables and
 can be solved graphically; its optimal value equals the primal optimum (strong duality), and the primal solution can be read
 from the final dual table or through complementary slackness. (c) Fix one variable and solve repeated two-variable cases
 only as a rough check.



2.5 Simplex algorithm

 The simplex method is an iterative algebraic procedure that starts at a BFS (an extreme point) and moves to an adjacent BFS
 that improves Z, stopping when no further improvement is possible.


Types of added variables: slack (≤, coefficient 0 in Z, gives the starting basis); surplus (≥, negative, coefficient 0); artificial (≥ and =
constraints, used only to get a starting basis, penalized in the objective).




Operations Research - Theory Notes Page 8 of 31

1. Convert to standard form (max problem; right-hand sides ≥ 0; add slack, surplus, artificial variables).

 2. Form the initial table with the starting BFS (slack or artificial variables basic).

 3. Compute Zj and Cj − Zj for every column.

 4. Optimality test: for Max, if all Cj − Zj ≤ 0, the solution is optimal. Otherwise continue. (For Min, optimal when all ≥ 0.)

 5. Entering variable: the non-basic variable with the most positive Cj − Zj (key column).

 6. Leaving variable (feasibility condition): minimum ratio = solution value / positive key-column entry (key row). The intersection
 is the pivot element.

 7. Divide the key row by the pivot and make the other entries of the key column zero by row operations. Repeat from step 3.

Tie-breaking: a tie in the entering variable is broken arbitrarily; a tie in the minimum ratio causes degeneracy in the next table.


2.6 Big-M method
Used when the constraints are ≥ or = (no obvious starting BFS). Each such constraint gets an artificial variable Ai with coefficient
−M in a Max problem (+M in a Min problem), where M is a very large positive number. The penalty forces artificial variables out
of the basis as the simplex proceeds.

 Rewrite constraints, add surplus (−S) and artificial (+A) variables; the starting basis is made of A's and slacks.

 Run simplex as usual; once an artificial variable leaves it never re-enters, and its column can be dropped.
 Infeasible problem: if an artificial variable is still in the final optimal basis at a positive level, the problem has no feasible
 solution.

Two-phase method (alternative): Phase I minimizes the sum of artificial variables; if the minimum is 0 a BFS of the original
problem is found, else infeasible. Phase II optimizes the true objective from that BFS. It avoids the large M.

2.8 Duality

 Every LP (the primal) has an associated LP (the dual) formed from the same data. Solving one solves the other.

Primal (Max) Dual (Min)

 Objective coefficients cj Right-hand sides of dual constraints

Duality results:

 Weak duality: for any feasible x and y, Zprimal(x) ≤ Wdual(y) for a max primal.

 Strong duality: if one problem has an optimal solution so does the other, and the optimal values are equal.

 Complementary slackness: at optimality, xj(dual slack of j) = 0 and yi(primal slack of i) = 0. A positive variable forces its partner
 constraint to be tight.

 The optimal dual values can be read from the Zj (or Cj − Zj) row of the final primal table under the slack columns.

Why use the dual: fewer rows when constraints outnumber variables; graphical solution when the primal has many variables but
few constraints; economic meaning (shadow prices); needed for sensitivity analysis and the dual simplex method.

Economic interpretation: yi is the value (shadow price) of one extra unit of resource i; the dual minimizes the total imputed worth
of resources such that each product's resource worth is at least its profit.


2.9 Dual simplex method
Used when a basic solution is optimal (all Cj − Zj correct sign) but infeasible (some right-hand side negative), as happens after
adding a new constraint or changing b. Unlike simplex, it keeps optimality and works towards feasibility.

 1. Convert all constraints to ≤ (multiply ≥ constraints by −1) and add slacks, giving an optimal but infeasible start.

 2. Leaving variable: the basic variable with the most negative right-hand side. If none, the solution is optimal and feasible.

 3. Entering variable: among negative entries in the key row, take the minimum of |(Cj − Zj) / arj|. If no negative entry exists, the
 problem is infeasible.

 4. Pivot and repeat.


2.10 Primal-dual algorithm
The primal-dual method starts with a dual feasible solution and works on the primal through a restricted primal problem that
uses only the dual constraints that are tight. If the restricted primal has a feasible solution (artificial sum = 0), both are optimal;



Operations Research - Theory Notes Page 10 of 31

otherwise the dual solution is improved by a step in the direction found from the restricted problem, and the process repeats. Its
advantage is that it avoids an explicit inverse and exploits network structure, so it is the basis of efficient transportation and
assignment algorithms.


2.11 Sensitivity analysis (post-optimality analysis)

 Sensitivity analysis studies how the optimal solution and the optimal value change when the input data (cj, bi, aij) change,
 without solving the problem again from the start.


Objectives: check the stability of the optimal solution; identify critical parameters; support decisions under uncertainty; guide
resource planning.

 Change in objective coefficient cj: the optimal basis stays optimal within the allowable increase / decrease. Graphically the
 slope of the objective line changes. Outside the range, the corner point changes.

 Change in right-hand side bi: the basis stays feasible within an allowable range; the optimum changes at a rate equal to the
 shadow price.

 Reduced cost: the amount by which the profit of a non-basic variable must improve before it enters the solution.
 Other changes: adding a new variable (compute its Cj − Zj with dual prices), adding a new constraint (check whether the
 current solution satisfies it, else use dual simplex), changing aij.


 Shadow price (dual value): the rate of change of the optimal objective value per unit increase in the right-hand side of a
 constraint, other data unchanged. It equals the optimal dual variable of that constraint.



 The sensitivity report shows a positive shadow price for a resource. Explain how the company can use this to decide
 whether to increase the availability of the resource and estimate the impact on total profit. Also write the dual of the
 given LP. 8 marks (theory part) Final Dec 2025

 MODEL ANSWER (THEORY PART)

 1. A positive shadow price y means the resource is scarce and fully used (binding constraint). One more unit raises profit
 by y.

 2. Decision rule: compare y with the cost of getting one extra unit. If cost per unit < y, buying more increases net profit; if
 cost > y, do not buy.

 3. Estimated impact: ΔZ ≈ y × Δb. This is valid only while Δb lies inside the allowable increase/decrease range for that right-
 hand side, because the optimal basis (and so y) stays unchanged only within that range. Beyond it, re-solve.

 4. Resources with zero shadow price have slack, so extra units add nothing. Shadow prices also rank resources: expand the
 one with the largest y first, and use y for pricing overtime or outsourcing.

 5. Assumptions: other data unchanged; one resource changed at a time (simultaneous changes need the 100% rule or a re-
 solve).

 Writing the dual: apply the rules table in 2.8: swap c and b, transpose A, flip the inequality directions and the Max/Min
 sense, and give each primal constraint a dual variable (sign by constraint type).

Unit 3 — Integer Programming Problem

3.1 Meaning and types

 An Integer Programming Problem (IPP) is an LP in which some or all decision variables must take integer values.


 Type Meaning

 Pure (all-) integer All variables must be integers

 Mixed integer Only some variables must be integers, the rest may be continuous

 0-1 (binary) integer Variables take only the values 0 or 1 (yes/no decisions)


Why not just round the LP answer? Rounding may give an infeasible point, or a feasible point that is far from the true integer
optimum. The LP relaxation (ignoring the integer condition) gives a bound: for Max, ZIP ≤ ZLP. The optimal integer value can never
be better than the relaxed value.

Where integers are needed: indivisible items (machines, vehicles, people), capital budgeting, plant location (0-1), job sequencing,
fixed-charge problems, travelling salesman.


3.2 Gomory's cutting plane method
Idea: solve the LP relaxation by simplex. If the answer is not integer, add a new linear constraint (a cut) that removes the current
fractional corner but removes no feasible integer point. Re-solve with dual simplex and repeat until all variables are integers.

 1. Solve the LP relaxation by simplex (ignore the integer condition). If the solution is integer, stop.

 2. Choose the row of a basic variable with a fractional value (the largest fractional part, ties broken arbitrarily). The row reads xB
 + Σ ajxj = b.

 3. Split every coefficient and b into integer part plus a non-negative fraction: aj = [aj] + fj, b = [b] + f0, with 0 ≤ f < 1. (For negative
 numbers, the fraction is still taken positive, e.g. −1.4 = −2 + 0.6.)

 4. Write the Gomory fractional cut: Σ fjxj ≥ f0, i.e. −Σ fjxj + sg = −f0 with a new slack sg ≥ 0.

 5. Add this row to the optimal table, which is now primal-infeasible (negative right-hand side) but optimal. Use dual simplex to
 restore feasibility.

 6. Check integrality again; repeat steps 2 to 5 till all required variables are integers.

Why the cut is valid: for integer x, the left side of the row equals an integer b minus an integer part, so Σ fjxj − f0 must be an
integer. Since the sum is non-negative and f0 < 1, it must be ≥ 0, giving Σ fjxj ≥ f0. The current LP optimum has all non-basic xj = 0,
so it violates the cut and is cut off.

Mixed-integer cut: when only some variables must be integer, the fractional-part cut is applied only to the row of an integer
variable, and continuous non-basic variables enter the cut through their own coefficients (positive coefficients as they are,
negative ones scaled by f0/(1−f0)). Integer non-basic variables use the fj form.

Features: needs the dual simplex after each cut; terminates in finite steps in theory but may need many cuts; round-off errors can
grow; gives an optimal integer solution when it ends.

3.3 Branch and bound method
Idea: a divide-and-conquer search. The feasible region is split (branched) into smaller sub-problems; each is solved as an LP to get
a bound on the best integer value it can contain; sub-problems that cannot beat the best integer solution found so far are
discarded (fathomed).

 1. Solve the LP relaxation. If integer, it is optimal. Else its Z gives the initial upper bound (Max) or lower bound (Min).

 2. Branch: pick a variable xk with fractional value v. Create two sub-problems: add xk ≤ [v] to one and xk ≥ [v] + 1 to the other.

 3. Solve each sub-problem as an LP.

 4. Fathom (stop branching) a node if: (a) its LP is infeasible; (b) its LP solution is integer (record it, update the incumbent, the
 best integer value so far); (c) its bound is no better than the incumbent.

 5. Branch again from a live node, usually the one with the best bound (for Max, the highest Z).

 6. Stop when no live node remains; the incumbent is optimal.

Branching rule: choose the variable with the largest fractional part (or the one with the largest objective coefficient). Search
strategies: depth-first (reaches an incumbent fast) or best-bound-first (fewer nodes).

 Basis Gomory cutting plane Branch and bound

 Approach Adds cuts to the same problem Splits into sub-problems (tree)

 LP solved One growing LP via dual simplex Many separate LPs

 Memory Small Large (many nodes)

 Numerical issues Round-off errors, slow convergence Robust; basis of commercial solvers

 Intermediate answers Not integer-feasible till the end Gives feasible incumbents early

 Handles mixed and 0-1 Mixed cut needed Easily

Unit 4 — Transportation and Assignment Problems

4.1 Transportation problem (TP)

 The transportation problem finds the least-cost plan to ship a single homogeneous commodity from m sources (supply ai) to
 n destinations (demand bj) when the unit cost cij of each route is known.


Mathematical model: Min Z = ΣΣ cijxij subject to Σj xij = ai (supply), Σi xij = bj (demand), xij ≥ 0. It is a special LP with m + n
constraints and m×n variables.

 Balanced TP: Σai = Σbj. Feasible solution: satisfies supply and demand. Basic feasible solution: a feasible solution with exactly
 m + n − 1 allocations in independent positions (no closed loop). Optimal: minimum total cost.
 One constraint is redundant in a balanced TP, which is why a BFS has m + n − 1 basic variables.

Steps: (1) balance the problem; (2) find an initial basic feasible solution; (3) test for optimality; (4) improve and repeat.


4.2 Initial basic feasible solution (IBFS) methods

 Describe the three methods used for finding an initial feasible solution to a transportation problem. What is the purpose
 of the MODI method? 4 marks Re-exam Feb 2025

 MODEL ANSWER (4 MARKS)

 1. North-West Corner Rule (NWCR): start at the top-left cell; allocate min(supply, demand); cross out the exhausted row or
 column; move right or down; repeat. It ignores costs, so it is the quickest but usually the most costly start.
 2. Least Cost Method (LCM, matrix minimum): allocate as much as possible to the cell with the smallest unit cost, cross
 out the satisfied row or column, then take the next cheapest remaining cell. It uses costs, so it is better than NWCR.

 3. Vogel's Approximation Method (VAM): for each row and column find the penalty = difference between the two
 smallest costs; select the row or column with the largest penalty; allocate to its cheapest cell; update penalties; repeat.
 It gives a start closest to the optimum.

 Purpose of MODI (u-v method): the Modified Distribution method tests whether a basic feasible solution is optimal. It finds
 ui and vj from allocated cells (ui + vj = cij) and computes the opportunity cost dij = cij − (ui + vj) for empty cells. If all dij ≥ 0
 the solution is optimal; otherwise it shows which cell should enter to reduce cost.


NWCR / LCM / VAM compared:


 Method Uses cost? Effort Quality of start

 NWCR No Lowest Poorest

 LCM Yes (smallest cell) Low Good

 VAM Yes (penalties = opportunity loss) Highest Best, often optimal or near-optimal


VAM tie-breaking: if penalties tie, choose the line having the cheapest cell, or the cell with the larger possible allocation.

4.3 Optimality test: MODI (u-v) method
 1. Make sure there are m + n − 1 allocated cells (add ε for degeneracy).

 2. Set one of ui or vj to 0 (usually the row with the most allocations). Solve ui + vj = cij for all allocated cells.

 3. For every empty cell compute the net evaluation (opportunity cost) dij = cij − (ui + vj).

 4. If all dij ≥ 0 (Min), the solution is optimal. A zero for an empty cell means an alternate optimum.

 5. Otherwise choose the most negative dij as the entering cell, draw the closed loop (stepping-stone path) through allocated
 cells with alternating + and − signs, shift the smallest − allocation (θ) around the loop, and re-test.

The stepping-stone method does the same test by evaluating the cost change of each empty cell through its loop; MODI avoids
drawing a loop for every empty cell.

4.5 Assignment problem (AP)

 The assignment problem is a special TP in which n jobs are assigned to n workers/machines on a one-to-one basis so that the

Model: Min Z = ΣΣ cijxij, Σj xij = 1, Σi xij = 1, xij = 0 or 1. Every supply and demand equals 1, so it is a TP with a degenerate structure

Key property: if a constant is added to or subtracted from every element of a row or a column of the cost matrix, the optimal
assignment is unchanged. The Hungarian method uses this to create zeros.


4.6 Hungarian method

 Explain how the Hungarian method is used to solve an assignment problem, considering both balanced and unbalanced

Operations Research - Theory Notes Page 15 of 31

MODEL ANSWER (4 MARKS)

 1. Balance the matrix: if the number of jobs ≠ number of workers (unbalanced), add dummy rows or columns with zero
 cost to make the matrix square. A balanced matrix is used as given.

 2. Row reduction: subtract the smallest element of each row from that row.

 3. Column reduction: subtract the smallest element of each column from that column. Now every row and column has at
 least one zero.

 4. Cover all zeros with the minimum number of horizontal/vertical lines.

 5. If the number of lines = n, an optimal assignment exists: go to step 7. If lines < n, revise: subtract the smallest uncovered
 element from all uncovered elements and add it to elements at line intersections; return to step 4.

 6. (Repeat until lines = n.)

 7. Make assignments: start with a row or column that has a single zero, assign it, strike out the other zeros of that row and
 column, and continue. The sum of the original costs of assigned cells is the minimum cost.

 Unbalanced case: a job assigned to a dummy worker is simply left unassigned (or a worker assigned to a dummy job is idle);
 the dummy has zero cost so the true cost is unaffected.

Unit 5 — Network Analysis (CPM and PERT)

5.1 Project and project management
A project is a set of related activities with a definite start and end, aimed at one objective. Project management covers planning,
scheduling, monitoring and controlling it. CPM (Kelley and Walker, 1957, chemical plant maintenance) and PERT (U.S. Navy Special
Projects Office, 1958, Polaris missile) are the two main network techniques. They answer: when will the project finish, which
activities are critical, which can slip without delay, what is the probability of finishing on a date, and how can it be shortened at
least cost.


5.2 Network terminology

 Term Meaning

 Activity A time- and resource-consuming task; shown by an arrow in the AOA diagram

 Event (node) A point in time marking the start or finish of activities; consumes no time

 Predecessor / successor Activity that must precede / follow another

 Dummy activity Dotted arrow with zero duration and no resource; used only to show a dependence or to give
 each activity a unique pair of end events

 Path Continuous chain of activities from the start to the end node

 Critical path The longest path; its length is the project duration; activities on it have zero total float

 Earliest start (ES) / finish (EF) Earliest time an activity can begin / end; EF = ES + t

 Latest start (LS) / finish (LF) Latest time it can begin / end without delaying the project; LS = LF − t

 Earliest event time (Ei), latest From the forward and backward pass
 event time (Lj)


Event-on-node (AON) vs event-on-arrow (AOA): in AOA (activity-on-arrow) activities are arrows between event nodes; in AON
(activity-on-node) activities are nodes and arrows show precedence, so dummies are not needed. Both give the same critical
path.

Rules for drawing a network: (1) one start and one end event; (2) each activity is one arrow with a unique head and tail event; (3)
no loops (cycles) and no dangling activities; (4) arrows are drawn left to right, and event numbers increase along the arrows (i < j,
Fulkerson's numbering); (5) use a dummy for common predecessors or to avoid two activities sharing the same end events; (6)
arrows should not cross unnecessarily.


5.3 Critical path computation
 1. Forward pass (left to right): E1 = 0; Ej = max over incoming activities (Ei + tij). Project duration = E of last node.

 2. Backward pass (right to left): L of last node = its E; Li = min over outgoing activities (Lj − tij).

 3. Activity times: ES = Ei, EF = ES + tij, LF = Lj, LS = LF − tij.




Operations Research - Theory Notes Page 18 of 31

4. Critical activities have Ei = Li, Ej = Lj and Lj − Ei = tij. The chain of these from start to end is the critical path (there may be more
 than one).


5.4 Floats (slack)

 Float Definition Formula

 Total float (TF) Time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project LS − ES = LF − EF = Lj − Ei − tij

 Free float (FF) Delay possible without affecting the start of any successor Ej − Ei − tij = TF − slack of head
 event

 Independent float Delay possible even when predecessors finish late and successors need the Ej − Li − tij (negative taken as 0)
 (IF) earliest start

 Interfering float Part of total float that, if used, affects successors TF − FF = Lj − Ej


Order: TF ≥ FF ≥ IF. Critical activities have TF = FF = IF = 0. Use of float: non-critical activities can be delayed, their resources shifted
to critical activities, and work levelled.


5.5 PERT: three time estimates and probability
 Optimistic time (to or a): shortest possible time if everything goes well.

 Most likely time (tm or m): the time most often needed under normal conditions (mode).

 Pessimistic time (tp or b): longest time if almost everything goes wrong.

Activity time is assumed to follow a Beta distribution:


 te = (to + 4tm + tp) / 6 σ2 = ((tp − to) / 6)2


Project expected duration = sum of te on the critical path; project variance = sum of the variances of critical activities (activities
assumed independent). Project duration is assumed approximately normal (central limit theorem). To find the probability of

completing by a due date Td: Z = (Td − Te) / σproject , then read P(Z) from the standard normal table. P(finish by Te) =

50%.

Limitations of PERT: the Beta and normal assumptions are approximate; the critical path may change as times are random
(merge-event bias, so true expected time is slightly higher); time estimates are subjective.

5.7 Project crashing and time-cost trade-off

 Define project crashing in CPM, and how does the time-cost trade-off concept work in this context? 4 marks
 Final Nov 2024

 Discuss the factors a project manager must consider before crashing activities. part of an 8-mark question Final Dec 2025

 MODEL ANSWER (4 TO 5 MARKS)

 Project crashing is the deliberate shortening of the project duration by reducing the time of selected activities, at extra cost,
 using more resources (overtime, extra labour, equipment, subcontracting). Normal time and cost (tn, Cn) correspond to
 normal resources; crash time and cost (tc, Cc) is the minimum possible duration and its cost.

 Time-cost trade-off:

 Direct costs (labour, material, equipment) rise as the project is shortened.
 Indirect costs (overheads, supervision, penalties) fall as duration falls.

 Total cost = direct + indirect is U-shaped; the optimum duration is at the minimum of the total cost curve, between
 normal and crash durations.


 Cost slope = (Cc − Cn) / (tn − tc) is the extra cost per unit time saved.


 Crashing procedure: (1) find the critical path with normal times; (2) compute the cost slope of every activity; (3) crash the
 critical activity with the lowest cost slope by one unit (up to its crash limit); (4) if several critical paths exist, crash all of
 them together (a common activity or one activity on each); (5) recompute the paths, as a non-critical path may become
 critical; (6) repeat until the required duration or the crash limit is reached, or when the cost of saving a day exceeds the
 indirect cost saved.

 Factors a project manager must consider before crashing:

 1. Crash only critical activities; crashing non-critical ones only wastes money.

 2. Cost slope of each activity against the saving in indirect cost and any delay penalty or early-completion bonus.
 3. Crash limit of each activity (technical minimum time).

 4. Parallel critical paths and how crashing changes which path is critical.

5. Resource availability (labour, equipment, budget) and whether extra resources can be mobilized in time.

 6. Quality and safety risk of working faster, and effect on worker morale.
 7. Contractual deadlines, client value of earlier completion, and the effect on dependent projects.

Unit 6 — Game Theory

6.1 Introduction and characteristics
Game theory studies decision making where several rational decision makers (players) have conflicting interests and each
outcome depends on the choices of all. It began with Cournot (1838); von Neumann and Morgenstern published Theory of Games
and Economic Behaviour (1944); John Nash introduced the Nash equilibrium.


 A game is an abstract model of a strategic situation involving interdependence, defined by players, strategies and payoffs.


Characteristics of a game:

 1. A finite number of competitors (players), two or more.

 2. Each player has a finite or infinite list of strategies (complete plans of action).
 3. Strict rules fix what moves are allowed.

 4. Each combination of strategies gives a definite payoff (gain or loss) to each player.
 5. Players act rationally: each tries to maximize own gain, expecting the opponent to do the same.

 6. The players' decisions are interdependent; the outcome is uncertain until choices are made.
 7. Each player knows all strategies and payoffs of both sides, but not the opponent's actual choice.

Terms: Payoff matrix: table of gains of the row player (maximizer) for every pair of strategies. Optimal strategy: the course of
action giving the best result regardless of the opponent. Value of the game (V): expected payoff to the maximizing player when
both play optimally. Fair game: V = 0. Strictly determinable game: has a saddle point, so a pure-strategy solution.

Types of games: two-person vs n-person; zero-sum (one player's gain is the other's loss, sum of payoffs = 0) vs non-zero-sum;
cooperative vs non-cooperative (binding agreements allowed or not); simultaneous vs sequential; finite vs infinite; perfect vs
imperfect information.


6.2 Two-person zero-sum game: maximin and minimax
Player A (rows) wants to maximize; B (columns) wants to minimize the same payoff. A is cautious: finds the minimum of each row,
then chooses the row with the largest minimum: maximin value (lower value of the game). B finds the maximum of each column
and chooses the column with the smallest: minimax value (upper value).


 maximin ≤ V ≤ minimax always. If maximin = minimax, the game has a saddle point: the entry that is the smallest in its

row and the largest in its column. The common value is V and the game is strictly determinable.

6.4 Pure and mixed strategies

 Define pure and mixed strategies in game theory and explain when a player would use a mixed strategy. 4 marks
 Final Nov 2024

 MODEL ANSWER (4 MARKS)

 Pure strategy: a player selects one particular course of action with certainty every time the game is played. The strategy is
 known and fixed; it is optimal when the game has a saddle point.

 Mixed strategy: a player selects among two or more pure strategies according to fixed probabilities, e.g. A plays A1 with
 probability p and A2 with 1 − p, with probabilities adding to 1. The choice on any play is random, so the opponent cannot
 predict or exploit it.

 When used: when there is no saddle point (maximin ≠ minimax), so no pure strategy is stable and any fixed choice can be
 exploited. The mixed strategy maximizes the player's expected payoff, and the value obtained lies between maximin and
 minimax. It is also suited to games repeated many times.



6.5 Solving a game without saddle point: mixed strategy methods
 2×2 game (algebraic / oddments): for payoff [[a, b], [c, d]] with no saddle point, p1 = (d − c) / (a + d − b − c), p2 = 1 − p1; q1 = (d
 − b) / (a + d − b − c), q2 = 1 − q1; V = (ad − bc) / (a + d − b − c). These come from equating A's expected payoff against each B
 strategy.
 Dominance principle: a strategy is dominated if another strategy is at least as good for its player in every case. For the row
 player, row i dominates row k if every entry of i ≥ the matching entry of k, so row k is deleted. For the column player
 (minimizer), column j dominates column l if every entry of j ≤ the matching entry of l, so column l is deleted. Also a strategy
 dominated by a convex combination (average) of others can be deleted. Dominance reduces the matrix before solving, often
 to 2×2.
 Graphical method (2×n or m×2): plot A's expected payoff against each of B's strategies as a function of p; the lower envelope's
 highest point (maximin) gives A's optimal mix; the two lines meeting there pick B's active strategies.

 Linear programming method: any m×n game can be written as a pair of dual LPs; the solution gives the mixed strategies and
 V.

Assumptions: two players; zero-sum; rational players; finite strategies; payoff matrix known; simultaneous choices. Limitations:
unrealistic perfect information and rationality; large games are hard to compute; many real conflicts are not zero-sum.


6.6 Nash equilibrium (from slides)
A strategy combination is a Nash equilibrium if each player's strategy is the best response to the others' strategies: no player
gains by changing alone. A saddle point of a zero-sum game is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Non-cooperative games with
finitely many strategies have an equilibrium in mixed strategies (Nash).

Unit 7 — Simulation and Sequencing

7.1 Simulation: definition and when it is used

 Simulation is a technique of performing experiments on a mathematical (computer) model that represents a real-life system,
 to study its behaviour under different conditions (Hira & Gupta).


It complements analytical methods when the system is too complex for closed-form solutions or randomness is important. Typical
uses: queuing, inventory control, production scheduling, project time estimation.

Steps in a simulation study:

 1. Problem definition 2. Model formulation 3. Data collection 4. Model coding


 5. Verification and validation 6. Experimental design 7. Output analysis 8. Implementation


 1. Problem definition: identify the system, objectives and performance measures.

 2. Model formulation: define the variables and their relationships.

 3. Data collection: gather statistical data for the random inputs (arrival, service, demand distributions).

 4. Model translation: code the logic in a language or package.

 5. Verification and validation: verification checks the program does what is intended; validation checks the model is realistic.

 6. Experimental design: choose alternatives to test, run length and number of runs.

 7. Output analysis: summarize and interpret results statistically (mean, variance).

 8. Implementation: apply the findings to the real system.


 Advantages Disadvantages

 Handles complex, random systems that analytical models Gives an estimate, not an exact or guaranteed optimum
 cannot

 Allows "what-if" tests without disturbing the real system Model building and coding can be costly and time consuming

 Cheaper and safer than experimenting on the real system Each run gives one sample, so many runs are needed for reliable
 results

 Compresses time (years in minutes) Results are only as good as the input data and model



7.2 Monte Carlo simulation and random numbers
Monte Carlo simulation uses random sampling from probability distributions to imitate a chance process. As the number of trials
grows, the simulated average converges to the theoretical expected value (e.g. a six-day run with a small sample can differ a lot
from E(X); 1000 days will be close).

Random number: a number in (0, 1) (or a digit string such as 00-99) generated so that every value in the range is equally
 likely and each number is independent of the others. It is used to represent random events like demand, service time or
 inter-arrival time.

 Properties: uniformly distributed on (0,1); statistically independent; uncorrelated in sequence; reproducible with the same
 seed; long cycle before repeating.

 Generation:

 1. Physical / manual methods: dice, cards, roulette wheel, printed random number tables (RAND 1955). Truly random but
 slow and not repeatable.
 2. Computational (pseudo-random) methods: a formula that looks random. The common one is the Linear Congruential
 Generator: Ri+1 = (aRi + c) mod m, ri = Ri / m, with seed R0, multiplier a, increment c and modulus m. Other methods:
 mid-square and mid-product methods.

 Pseudo-random numbers are preferred in computers because they are fast, repeatable, and need no storage.

7.3 Discrete event system simulation (DESS)
DESS models systems whose state changes only at discrete instants when events occur: a customer arrives, a service ends, stock
reaches the reorder level. It models, analyses and optimizes complex time-evolving systems.

Component Meaning

 System state Values of all variables describing the system at a time (e.g. server busy or idle, queue length)

 Event Instantaneous occurrence that changes the state (arrival, departure)

 Simulation clock Records simulated time; it jumps from one event time to the next (next-event time advance) rather than

 Event list (future All scheduled future events sorted by time. Operations: insert a new event, remove the next event to execute,
 event list) keep it ordered (priority queue / min-heap). It decides which event is next

 Statistical counters Accumulate performance measures: waiting time, server utilization, queue length


How it works (single-server example): initialize clock = 0 and the event list with the first arrival. Repeat: take the earliest event
from the list; advance the clock to its time; update the state and counters; schedule new events (an arrival schedules the next
arrival and, if the server is free, its own departure; a departure starts service for the next waiting customer, if any); stop at the end
time.

Applications:

 Scheduling: events are job arrival and machine start/finish; finds bottlenecks and compares rules such as FIFO and shortest job
 first; goal is lower idle time and higher throughput.
 Queuing systems (bank, call centre, hospital desk): arrival, service start and end; measures average wait, queue length, server
 utilization; helps fix staffing levels.

 Inventory systems: demand, reorder placement, order arrival; measures stock-out probability, average inventory, ordering
 cost; helps choose reorder point and order quantity.

Benefits: models randomness, supports what-if analysis without disrupting the real system, low cost for testing new policies.


7.4 Sequencing (job scheduling)

 Sequencing is the selection of the order in which n jobs are processed on a finite number of machines so as to optimize a
 measure such as total elapsed time, idle time, cost or tardiness.


Terms: Processing time tij of job i on machine j. Total elapsed time: time from starting the first job to completing the last job on
the last machine. Idle time of a machine: time it waits with no job between start and end. Processing order: the order of machines
for each job. Sequence: order of jobs.

Assumptions: processing times are known and fixed; independent of sequence; a job is processed on one machine at a time and a
machine handles one job at a time; once started a job is not interrupted; no priorities; transfer time negligible; all jobs are
available at the start.

Number of schedules: n jobs on m machines give (n!)m possible schedules, so a rule is needed (e.g. 5 jobs, 5 machines: about 25
billion). With one machine, total time is the same for any sequence; sequence matters only with set-up times, due dates or flow
times.

Common sequencing rules: FCFS (first come first served); SPT (shortest processing time; minimizes mean flow time); EDD (earliest
due date; minimizes maximum lateness); CR (critical ratio; in the course slides CR = processing time / time remaining to due date
and the job with the largest CR goes next; textbooks often use the inverse, time remaining / work remaining, and take the
smallest).

7.5 Processing n jobs through two machines: Johnson's rule

 Describe how to process n jobs through two machines in a production system. 4 marks Final Nov 2024

 MODEL ANSWER (4 MARKS)
 Problem: n jobs each need machine M1 first and then M2. Choose the order that minimizes total elapsed time and machine
 idle time. Johnson's rule gives the optimal order.

 1. List the processing times of all jobs on M1 and M2.

 2. Find the smallest time among all the times not yet scheduled.

 3. If it is on M1, place that job as early as possible (at the front of the sequence). If it is on M2, place it as late as possible
 (at the back).

 4. Remove the scheduled job and repeat from step 2 for the remaining positions. A tie is broken arbitrarily (ties between
 M1 and M2: choose M1; ties among jobs: any).

 5. With the final sequence, draw the schedule (Gantt chart) to find total elapsed time and idle time of each machine.

 Conditions: times known and constant; independent of sequence; every job follows the same order M1 then M2; no job
 priority; a job finishes on M1 before starting on M2. Why it works: small M1 times at the start get M2 working early, and
 small M2 times at the end shorten M1's lead needed, minimizing M2 idle time.



7.6 Processing n jobs through three machines
No general rule exists, but Johnson's rule can be applied when the following condition holds for processing times on machines A,
B, C:


 min(Ai) ≥ max(Bi) or min(Ci) ≥ max(Bi)


 1. Check the condition (the middle machine B must be dominated).

 2. Create two fictitious (virtual) machines: G with time Ai + Bi, and H with time Bi + Ci.

 3. Apply Johnson's two-machine rule to G and H to get the sequence.

 4. Compute total elapsed time and idle times using the original three-machine times.

If the condition fails, the method gives only an approximate or trial sequence; use enumeration, branch and bound or heuristics.


7.7 Processing n jobs through m machines
For m machines (m > 3) with every job following the same machine order, the problem is solved by extending the three-machine
idea: if min time on the first machine and on the last machine each are at least the maximum time on every middle machine (min
ti1 ≥ max tij or min tim ≥ max tij for j = 2, ..., m−1), form two fictitious machines G = ti1 + ti2 + ... + ti,m−1 and H = ti2 + ... + tim and

use Johnson's rule. If the condition does not hold, exact solution is hard because there are (n!)m schedules; heuristics (e.g.
Palmer's slope index, CDS) or branch and bound are used.

Other cases from the unit: one machine, many jobs (total time independent of sequence; use SPT/EDD for flow time or lateness);
two machines, many jobs (Johnson); three machines (conditional Johnson); many machines, many jobs (heuristics, simulation).
